item.text:
I completed a broad continuation pass across all eight selected chapters without scoring Prayut Chanocha. The workspace was read-only and repository commands failed at sandbox startup, so I could not persist changes to the notebook or `research-ledger-manifest.json`. The following is the permissive research handoff to append.

### 1B — Political freedom

- `THA-2023-1B-01`: ANFREL reported that the 14 May election had 75.22% turnout, broad public acceptance, and improved accountability, transparency, and inclusiveness versus 2019. Attribution: formal government/election administration. [ANFREL final-report summary](https://anfrel.org/2023-thai-general-election-democracy-at-a-crossroads/)
- `THA-2023-1B-02`: ANFREL nevertheless identified vote-buying concerns and continuing weaknesses in electoral quality and transparency. Attribution: institutional responsibility of the Prayut-era state. Same source.
- `THA-2023-1B-03`: Human Rights Watch reported that at least 1,928 people had been prosecuted for expression or peaceful assembly since July 2020, with prosecutions continuing through September 2023. Attribution: government enforcement and judiciary. [HRW World Report 2024](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/thailand)
- `THA-2023-1B-04`: Arnon Nampa was sentenced to four years in September 2023 for lèse-majesté-related speech. Attribution: court action under laws maintained by the state. Same source.
- `THA-2023-1B-05`: A newly elected Move Forward MP, Rukchanok Srinok, received a six-year sentence in December 2023 over two social-media posts. Attribution: judicial enforcement; not evidence of a personal Prayut order. [AP report](https://apnews.com/article/5714eea2b3a55df891de9b4e658366ac)

Contrary evidence: the campaign was competitive, turnout was high, and the election was conducted without significant campaign violence. This chapter has recoverable evidence but mixed liberalization and repression signals.

### 2B — Corruption

- `THA-2023-2B-01`: Thailand scored 35/100 and ranked 108th of 180 in Transparency International’s 2023 CPI, declining one point from 2022. [Transparency International CPI 2023](https://www.transparency.org/en/cpi/2023/index/tha)
- `THA-2023-2B-02`: The US State Department’s 2023 human-rights report identified serious government corruption and political interference in the judiciary. Attribution: national governance environment during the target year. [2023 Thailand report](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2107649.html)
- `THA-2023-2B-03`: Thailand’s State Audit Office reported performance audits covering 520.68 billion baht and protection of more than 30 billion baht in public funds. Attribution: formal anti-corruption and oversight capacity. [Thai State Audit Office](https://www.audit.go.th/eng/node/14608)
- `THA-2023-2B-04`: The World Bank called for improved spending efficiency, revenue collection, and transparency while keeping public debt under control. This is reform evidence and also identifies unresolved governance weaknesses. [World Bank, May 2023](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/05/29/increased-revenue-required-to-meet-public-spending-needs)

Contrary evidence: functioning audit institutions and reported recoveries provide evidence of capacity, but not proof that corruption was reduced.

### 3B — Economic performance

- `THA-2023-3B-01`: The World Bank reported 4.5% year-on-year growth in 2023 Q1, driven by domestic demand and tourism. [Thailand Economic Monitor, June 2023](https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/thailand/publication/thailand-economic-monitor-june-2023-coping-with-floods-and-droughts)
- `THA-2023-3B-02`: The same report said Thailand’s recovery still lagged regional peers and that political transition could delay public investment.
- `THA-2023-3B-03`: The IMF’s retrospective 2023 Article IV assessment estimated real GDP growth at 2.5% and average headline inflation at 1.3%. [IMF 2023 Article IV](https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2024/01/22/pr2420-tha-imf-executive-board-concludes-2023-article-iv-consultation-with-thailand)
- `THA-2023-3B-04`: The World Bank projected 3.9% growth in June 2023, supported by tourism, private consumption, and external demand, while warning about fiscal and climate pressures. [World Bank June 2023 release](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/06/28/thai-economy-to-accelerate-in-2023-as-demand-from-major-economies-picks-up)
- `THA-2023-3B-05`: The World Bank identified flood and drought exposure, especially in the poorer northeast, as a material constraint on inclusive growth.

Contrary evidence: growth resumed and inflation remained moderate; the main shortfall is slower-than-peer recovery and limited evidence tying outcomes specifically to Prayut rather than inherited or structural conditions.

### 4B — Domestic violence

- `THA-2023-4B-01`: Thailand’s Statistical Yearbook records 2023 domestic-violence incidents by category, including physical assault, threats, abandonment, rape, and detention. [Thailand Statistical Yearbook 2024, table 7.8](https://www.nso.go.th/public/e-book/Statistical-Yearbook/SYB-2024/284/)
- `THA-2023-4B-02`: UN Women reports that the National Action Plan for Elimination of Violence Against Women 2023–2027 was still under development. [UN Women Thailand profile](https://data.unwomen.org/global-database-on-violence-against-women/country-profile/Thailand/country-snapshot)
- `THA-2023-4B-03`: Thailand’s Ministry of Social Development hotline recorded 12,490 violence cases across 2020–2023. This demonstrates reporting and service demand, not prevalence alone. [UN Women administrative-data page](https://data.unwomen.org/global-database-on-violence-against-women/country-profile/Thailand/measures/Administrative%20Data%20on%20Gender%20and%20Age%20Dimensions%20of%20Reported%20Violence)
- `THA-2023-4B-04`: The US State Department identified extensive gender-based, domestic, intimate-partner, and sexual violence in its 2023 country assessment. [2023 Thailand report](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2107649.html)
- `THA-2023-4B-05`: UN Women documented survivor-centred service coordination and local task-force activity with Thai authorities, including migrant-worker support.

Contrary evidence: hotline systems, task forces, and planned national action show institutional response. Target-year ruler attribution is limited to formal government responsibility; individual-order evidence was not recovered.

### 5B — Peace and internal violence

- `THA-2023-5B-01`: Crisis Group reported that the southern peace dialogue stalled after the BRN failed to participate and the planned June 2023 roadmap became impracticable. [Crisis Group, Southern Thailand’s Stop-start Peace Dialogue, p. 8](https://www.crisisgroup.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/b176-southern-thailands-peace-dialogue.pdf)
- `THA-2023-5B-02`: Crisis Group documented April 2023 attacks in Yala, Pattani, and Narathiwat, including attacks on security posts, bombings, shootings, and killings.
- `THA-2023-5B-03`: The US terrorism report said insurgent attacks likely increased slightly in 2023 and remained concentrated in the southernmost provinces. [US State Department terrorism report](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2119009.html)
- `THA-2023-5B-04`: Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim met Prayut in February 2023 and offered Malaysian assistance in resolving the southern insurgency. [AP report](https://apnews.com/article/ec28a896b55e42e564aa6c1d7ceff760)
- `THA-2023-5B-05`: Crisis Group records that the Thai delegation proposed a Ramadan cessation-of-hostilities message and delivered a revised joint peace-process document, but BRN did not reciprocate.

Contrary evidence: mediation and formal dialogue continued intermittently, and some reported attacks caused no casualties. The conflict remained unresolved during the target period.

### 6B — Nuclear policy

- `THA-2023-6B-01`: Thailand is a non-nuclear-weapon state and acceded to the NPT in 1972. [NTI NPT record](https://www.nti.org/education-center/treaties-and-regimes/treaty-on-the-non-proliferation-of-nuclear-weapons/)
- `THA-2023-6B-02`: Thailand is a party to the Southeast Asian Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty. [NTI Bangkok Treaty record](https://www.nti.org/education-center/treaties-and-regimes/southeast-asian-nuclear-weapon-free-zone-seanwfz-treaty-bangkok-treaty/)
- `THA-2023-6B-03`: NTI’s 2023 Nuclear Security Index listed Thailand at 80 points, six points higher than the prior edition. [NTI 2023 Index](https://www.nti.org/analysis/articles/the-2023-nti-nuclear-security-index/)
- `THA-2023-6B-04`: No credible 2023 evidence was found of a Thai nuclear-weapons program, nuclear coercion, or a Prayut-specific proliferation decision.

Honest shortfall: only four defensible units were recovered, and most are persistent treaty/institutional facts rather than 2023 events.

### 7B — External/security conduct

- `THA-2023-7B-01`: Thailand participated in Malaysia-facilitated southern peace diplomacy while maintaining counterinsurgency operations. The record shows both negotiation and continued coercive security policy. [Crisis Group report](https://www.crisisgroup.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/b176-southern-thailands-peace-dialogue.pdf)
- `THA-2023-7B-02`: Thailand abstained on a 2023 UN resolution concerning Myanmar, while the caretaker government separately initiated informal regional peace talks with Myanmar’s junta. [TIME report](https://time.com/6326274/asean-myanmar-junta-trade/)
- `THA-2023-7B-03`: The government announced an intention to seek a UN Human Rights Council seat for 2025–2027 despite unresolved rights concerns. [HRW World Report 2023](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/thailand)
- `THA-2023-7B-04`: Thailand’s 2023 military expenditure was reported at approximately 1.17% of GDP, while the FY2023 defence allocation was approximately 197.29 billion baht. [SIPRI Thailand budget page](https://www.sipri.org/national-budget-report/thailand/2023)

Attribution is authority-based: these were state-level foreign, security, and defence policies during Prayut’s final caretaker period, not necessarily personally ordered by him.

### 8B — Government effectiveness

- `THA-2023-8B-01`: The State Audit Office reported audits of large-scale government spending across environment, economy, utilities, health, and education, indicating functioning oversight machinery. [SAO performance report](https://www.audit.go.th/eng/node/14608)
- `THA-2023-8B-02`: The World Bank warned that fiscal constraints, weak revenue mobilisation, and growing spending needs threatened service delivery and public investment. [World Bank public-spending assessment](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/05/29/increased-revenue-required-to-meet-public-spending-needs)
- `THA-2023-8B-03`: The World Bank reported that the prolonged political transition could delay public investment. [Thailand Economic Monitor](https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/thailand/publication/thailand-economic-monitor-june-2023-coping-with-floods-and-droughts)
- `THA-2023-8B-04`: Election administration achieved an orderly nationwide vote with high turnout, although observers identified tabulation-access and procedural weaknesses. [ANFREL interim report](https://anfrel.org/anfrel-ieom-to-the-2023-thai-general-election-interim-report/)
- `THA-2023-8B-05`: The World Bank’s later country assessment says growth gained momentum in 2022–23 but that Thailand still needs more inclusive, accountable, and transparent public services. [World Bank SCD update](https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/thailand/publication/thailand-scd2024)

Contrary evidence: administrative capacity was visible in elections, audits, and economic recovery. Effectiveness was constrained by political transition, fiscal pressure, uneven service delivery, and unresolved security problems.

Recommended ledger dispositions: add all units above as `accepted_provisional`; mark the NTI/treaty items as `persistent_context`; mark the AP, HRW, and State Department items as `authority_based`; mark the absence of a personal order as `attribution_limited`; and retain all contrary-evidence notes.
